deep.lede: Jesus' words over the bread and cup survive in four early versions: Mark, Matthew, Luke, and Paul's First Letter to the Corinthians (11:23–25), written about twenty years before Mark. Laid side by side, they fall into two families, and the differences show how a sacred formula was handed on and shaped in worship.

sections.heading: Two families of wording
sections.body:
Matthew follows Mark closely here; the alignment above shows about 70% of Matthew's words taken from Mark. Mark's bread-word is bare: {mk 14:22 Λάβετε τοῦτό ἐστιν τὸ σῶμά μου} (“take, this is my body”). Matthew adds one verb, {mt 26:26 φάγετε} (“eat”), and turns Mark's narration that “they all drank” into a command, {mt 26:27 Πίετε ἐξ αὐτοῦ πάντες} (“drink from it, all of you”). Both read like the words of a liturgy.

Luke belongs to the other family, the one Paul also quotes. His bread is {lk 22:19 τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν διδόμενον} (“given **for you**”), followed by {lk 22:19 τοῦτο ποιεῖτε εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν} (“do this in remembrance of me”). The command to remember appears only in Luke and Paul. His cup is {lk 22:20 ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐν τῷ αἵματί μου} (“the new covenant in my blood”), recalling Jeremiah 31's promise of a new covenant, where Mark's {mk 14:24 τὸ αἷμά μου τῆς διαθήκης} recalls Moses sprinkling “the blood of the covenant” at Sinai (Exodus 24:8).

sections.heading: Luke's two cups, and a famous textual problem
sections.body:
Only Luke has a cup **before** the bread: {lk 22:17 Λάβετε τοῦτο καὶ διαμερίσατε εἰς ἑαυτούς} (“take this and share it among yourselves”), and then a second cup {lk 22:20 μετὰ τὸ δειπνῆσαι} (“after supper”). A Passover meal involved several cups of wine, so the sequence may reflect the meal's real shape.

There is a complication. Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts lack everything from “given for you” to the end of verse 20, which leaves Luke with a cup-then-bread order. In the nineteenth century Westcott and Hort counted the longer text as a later addition. The discovery of the early papyrus P75, which contains it, has persuaded most modern editors that it is original.

sections.heading: A meal that looks forward
sections.body: All three Synoptics keep a vow that points beyond the meal. Jesus will not drink again {mk 14:25 ἐκ τοῦ γενήματος τῆς ἀμπέλου} (“of the fruit of the vine”) until he drinks it new in the kingdom of God. Matthew adds two words that turn it into a promise of reunion: {mt 26:29 μεθ ὑμῶν} (“**with you**”). Luke moves the vow before the bread, so that his supper begins with the end of the age in view: Jesus will not eat the Passover again {lk 22:16 ἕως ὅτου πληρωθῇ ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ} (“until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God”).

sections.heading: Matthew's addition, John's silence
sections.body:
Matthew's cup is poured out {mt 26:28 εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν} (“for the forgiveness of sins”). Mark had used that phrase for John the Baptist's baptism (1:4), and Matthew left it out there. He seems to have kept it for this moment, so that forgiveness is tied to Jesus' death rather than John's water.

John's Gospel tells the Last Supper across five chapters, yet it has no words over bread and cup at all. In their place is the foot-washing, and the eucharistic language appears instead in the Bread of Life discourse after the feeding of the five thousand (6:51–58). Whether John assumes his readers know the ritual, or deliberately moves its meaning elsewhere, is an open question.

deep.lede: No scene shows the Gospels' different portraits of Jesus more clearly than the night in Gethsemane. Mark's Jesus is overwhelmed, Matthew's prays the Lord's Prayer, and Luke's, in the oldest manuscripts, is composed. John leaves out the struggle altogether.

sections.heading: Mark: horror and the Aramaic word for Father
sections.body:
Mark uses strong verbs: Jesus {mk 14:33 ἤρξατο ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι καὶ ἀδημονεῖν} (“began to be utterly dismayed and distressed”). He says {mk 14:34 Περίλυπός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου ἕως θανάτου} (“my soul is deeply grieved, to the point of death”), borrowing the refrain of Psalms 42–43. He does not kneel; he {mk 14:35 ἔπιπτεν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς} (“kept falling to the ground”).

The prayer opens with {mk 14:36 Αββα ὁ πατήρ}, the Aramaic *abba* followed by its Greek equivalent. Paul uses exactly this pair as the prayer of believers (Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:6), which suggests that early Greek-speaking Christians remembered and repeated Jesus' own word.

sections.heading: Matthew: the Lord's Prayer under pressure
sections.body: Matthew keeps Mark's structure of three returns to the sleeping disciples, but gives the second prayer its own words: {mt 26:42 γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου} (“your will be done”). That is word for word the third petition of the Lord's Prayer as Matthew records it (6:10). Matthew's Jesus prays in his darkest hour the prayer he taught on the mountain, and the reader who knows the Sermon hears the echo.

sections.heading: Luke: kneeling, and two disputed verses
sections.body:
Luke's account is shorter and calmer. Jesus withdraws {lk 22:41 ὡσεὶ λίθου βολήν} (“about a stone's throw”) and {lk 22:41 θεὶς τὰ γόνατα} (“knelt”), the posture of prayer in Acts. There is one prayer, not three: {lk 22:42 πλὴν μὴ τὸ θέλημά μου ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν γινέσθω} (“yet not my will but yours be done”). Luke even excuses the disciples, who are sleeping {lk 22:45 ἀπὸ τῆς λύπης} (“from grief”).

Then come the most debated verses in Luke's Passion: an angel strengthening Jesus ({lk 22:43 ὤφθη δὲ αὐτῷ ἄγγελος}) and {lk 22:44 ὁ ἱδρὼς αὐτοῦ ὡσεὶ θρόμβοι αἵματος} (“his sweat became **like** drops of blood”; a simile, not a medical claim). They are missing from P75 and Codex Vaticanus. Some scholars argue that they don't fit Luke's otherwise composed Jesus and were added; others, that orthodox scribes cut them because they made Jesus look too weak. The site's data marks them as doubtful text.

sections.heading: John: the cup accepted
sections.body: John has no agony in the garden. His Jesus addressed the temptation earlier, rhetorically: “shall I say, ‘Father, save me from this hour’? No, for this purpose I came” (12:27). At the arrest the Synoptic prayer about the cup is turned into its opposite: {jn 18:11 τὸ ποτήριον ὃ δέδωκέν μοι ὁ πατὴρ οὐ μὴ πίω αὐτό} (“the cup the Father has given me, shall I not drink it?”). The tradition is the same, but the Christology has changed: in John, Jesus is never a victim of his hour, only its master.

deep.lede: Peter's denial is one of the few stories told in all four Gospels with the same skeleton: a courtyard, a fire, three challenges, a rooster. It is also embarrassing to the movement's leading apostle, which most historians count as a mark of authenticity. The details each evangelist adds show what each wanted the story to mean.

sections.heading: Mark: two scenes at once
sections.body:
Mark sets up a split screen. Peter follows {mk 14:54 ἀπὸ μακρόθεν} (“at a distance”) and sits with the guards {mk 14:54 θερμαινόμενος} (“warming himself”) while Jesus is tried inside. Then Mark cuts back and forth. Inside, Jesus answers the high priest with “I am”. Outside, Peter's answers escalate. First comes a lawyerly dodge, {mk 14:68 Οὔτε οἶδα οὔτε ἐπίσταμαι σὺ τί λέγεις} (“I neither know nor understand what you mean”); then {mk 14:71 ἤρξατο ἀναθεματίζειν καὶ ὀμνύναι} (“he began to curse and swear”). The verb *anathematizein* has no object. Some scholars suggest that Peter was cursing Jesus, the ultimate denial, and that Mark tactfully left the object out.

Mark alone has the rooster crow twice, and ends with a puzzling phrase: {mk 14:72 ἐπιβαλὼν ἔκλαιεν}, perhaps “he broke down and wept”. The meaning of *epibalōn* here is genuinely uncertain.

sections.heading: A minor agreement in tears
sections.body: Matthew and Luke both replace Mark's obscure ending with the same five words: {mt 26:75 ἐξελθὼν ἔξω ἔκλαυσεν πικρῶς} and {lk 22:62 ἐξελθὼν ἔξω ἔκλαυσεν πικρῶς} (“going outside, he wept bitterly”). Two independent editors could each have clarified Mark, but finding the **identical** five-word solution is harder to explain. Two-Source scholars point out that a few Old Latin manuscripts lack Luke 22:62, and argue that a scribe borrowed it from Matthew. On the Farrer view, Luke simply took it from Matthew.

sections.heading: Luke: firelight and a look
sections.body: Luke tells the denials **before** the trial, so they are not interleaved with it, and he softens Peter's words: there are no curses. He adds lighting, as a novelist might: the servant girl sees Peter {lk 22:56 πρὸς τὸ φῶς} (“facing the firelight”) and stares. And he adds the most quoted detail of all: {lk 22:61 στραφεὶς ὁ κύριος ἐνέβλεψεν τῷ Πέτρῳ} (“the Lord turned and looked at Peter”). In Luke, Jesus is close enough to see him, which makes the moment personal rather than merely tragic.

sections.heading: John: “I am not”, and a second charcoal fire
sections.body: John shapes the story with contrast. In the garden Jesus has just said “I am” (*egō eimi*) three times; in the courtyard Peter answers twice {jn 18:25 Οὐκ εἰμί} (“I am **not**”). John's fire is an {jn 18:18 ἀνθρακιὰν} (“a charcoal fire”). The word appears only one other time in the New Testament: on the beach after the resurrection, where the risen Jesus has made {jn 21:9 ἀνθρακιὰν} and asks Peter {jn 21:17 τὸ τρίτον} (“a third time”), “do you love me?” Three denials beside one charcoal fire are answered by three affirmations beside another.

deep.lede: The Jewish hearing is reported in three very different shapes. Mark and Matthew describe a night trial with witnesses and a death verdict; Luke, a morning session that issues no verdict; John, an informal interrogation by a former high priest. Inside this unit is also one of the most debated minor agreements in the Synoptic problem.

sections.heading: Mark: the secret comes out
sections.body:
Mark's trial begins as a failure: the witnesses' testimony is inconsistent, {mk 14:56 ἴσαι αἱ μαρτυρίαι οὐκ ἦσαν} (“their testimonies did not agree”), and Deuteronomy 19:15 required two witnesses who agreed. The high priest then asks directly, with a reverent substitute for God's name: {mk 14:61 Σὺ εἶ ὁ χριστὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ εὐλογητοῦ} (“are you the Christ, the Son of the **Blessed One**?”).

All through Mark, Jesus has silenced those who named him. Now, at the moment it will cost him his life, he answers without qualification: {mk 14:62 Ἐγώ εἰμι} (“I am”). He then combines Daniel 7:13 and Psalm 110:1, the Son of Man seated at the right hand and coming with the clouds. The high priest tears his garments, and the verdict is {mk 14:64 ἔνοχον εἶναι θανάτου} (“deserving death”).

sections.heading: Matthew and Luke: a guarded answer
sections.body:
Both later Gospels make the answer less direct. In Matthew the high priest puts Jesus under oath, {mt 26:63 Ἐξορκίζω σε κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶντος} (“I adjure you by the living God”), and Jesus replies {mt 26:64 Σὺ εἶπας} (“you have said it”). Luke splits the question in two, and Jesus first refuses: {lk 22:67 Ἐὰν ὑμῖν εἴπω οὐ μὴ πιστεύσητε} (“if I tell you, you will not believe”). Then {lk 22:70 Ὑμεῖς λέγετε ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι} (“you say that I am”).

Both add a time marker Mark lacks: Matthew's {mt 26:64 ἀπ ἄρτι} and Luke's {lk 22:69 ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν}, each meaning “from now on”. Luke also drops the coming on the clouds: {lk 22:69 ἔσται ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καθήμενος} (“the Son of Man will be **seated**”). The exaltation begins now, and the return can wait, a pattern seen throughout Luke–Acts.

sections.heading: “Who is it that struck you?”
sections.body:
In Mark the guards cover Jesus' face, strike him, and say {mk 14:65 Προφήτευσον} (“Prophesy!”). Matthew and Luke both add the same five Greek words: {mt 26:68 τίς ἐστιν ὁ παίσας σε} and {lk 22:64 τίς ἐστιν ὁ παίσας σε} (“who is it that struck you?”). In Luke the taunt makes sense, because he keeps the blindfold. Matthew has dropped the blindfold, so his guards demand that Jesus identify someone he can plainly see.

For the Two-Source hypothesis, which holds that Matthew and Luke used Mark independently, this is a hard case. Its defenders suggest that early scribes copied the line into Matthew from Luke, though no surviving manuscript of Matthew lacks it, or that both drew on a common oral version of the mockery. For Farrer and Griesbach advocates it is simple: one evangelist read the other.

sections.heading: John: no trial at all
sections.body: John has no session of the council and no verdict. Jesus is taken {jn 18:13 πρὸς Ἅνναν πρῶτον} (“to Annas first”), the former high priest and father-in-law of Caiaphas, who questions him about his teaching. Jesus answers {jn 18:20 Ἐγὼ παρρησίᾳ λελάληκα τῷ κόσμῳ} (“I have spoken openly to the world”). In John the decision was already made back in chapter 11, after Lazarus was raised, and the whole Gospel has been a trial, with witnesses called and testimony given. The night hearing is a formality.

deep.lede: Pilate's first question is identical, word for word, in all four Gospels: {mk 15:2 Σὺ εἶ ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων} (“are you the King of the Jews?”). That is very rare across the Synoptics and John, and it suggests a fixed early memory. The charge on which Rome executed Jesus was a political one. From that shared starting point, each Gospel builds a very different trial.

sections.heading: The shared core: two words and a silence
sections.body: All three Synoptics give the same two-word reply: {mt 27:11 Σὺ λέγεις}, {lk 23:3 Σὺ λέγεις} (“you say so”). It is neither yes nor no. Then, in Mark and Matthew, Jesus says nothing more, {mk 15:5 ὥστε θαυμάζειν τὸν Πιλᾶτον} (“so that Pilate was amazed”). Early Christians heard Isaiah 53:7 in the silence: “like a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he did not open his mouth.”

sections.heading: Luke: a political trial and three acquittals
sections.body:
Luke gives the accusers a precise indictment with three counts: {lk 23:2 διαστρέφοντα τὸ ἔθνος ἡμῶν} (“subverting our nation”), forbidding taxes to Caesar, and claiming to be a king. Readers know the second count is false, because Jesus had said “give to Caesar what is Caesar's” (20:25).

Luke then has Pilate declare Jesus innocent three times, ending with {lk 23:22 ὁ δὲ τρίτον εἶπεν} (“a third time he said”): “I have found in him no cause for death.” The pattern matches Acts, where Roman officials repeatedly find Paul innocent. Many scholars see an apologetic aim: to show Roman readers that the movement's founder was no rebel, whatever the cross implied.

sections.heading: John: inside and outside
sections.body:
John stages the trial as a drama on two levels. Pilate goes back and forth between the accusers outside, who will not enter, and Jesus inside: {jn 18:33 Εἰσῆλθεν οὖν πάλιν εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον} (“so Pilate went back into the praetorium”). Many commentators count seven alternating scenes. Inside, Jesus explains his kingship: {jn 18:36 Ἡ βασιλεία ἡ ἐμὴ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου}. The preposition *ek* means “**from** this world”, its source, not that it is absent from this world.

John expands the Synoptic reply into a statement: {jn 18:37 Σὺ λέγεις ὅτι βασιλεύς εἰμι} (“you say that I am a king”), “for this I was born, to testify to the truth.” Pilate's reply, {jn 18:38 Τί ἐστιν ἀλήθεια} (“what is truth?”), gets no answer, and John's irony is that the person standing in front of him has already claimed to be the truth (14:6). By the end of the scene, the reader suspects that the judge is the one on trial.

deep.lede: Every Gospel includes the Barabbas episode, and none of them agrees with the others about who was to blame. Read in sequence, they show a steady shift: Pilate is made more reluctant and the Jewish crowd more responsible. That shift had grave consequences in later history.

sections.heading: An amnesty and a rebel
sections.body: Mark describes a custom: {mk 15:6 Κατὰ δὲ ἑορτὴν ἀπέλυεν αὐτοῖς ἕνα δέσμιον} (“at the festival he used to release one prisoner for them”). No source outside the Gospels mentions such a Passover amnesty, and historians debate it. Defenders note how sparse the sources are, and that the Mishnah (Pesachim 8:6) allows a Passover lamb to be slaughtered for someone promised release from prison. Barabbas is no ordinary prisoner. Mark places him {mk 15:7 μετὰ τῶν στασιαστῶν δεδεμένος} (“imprisoned with the insurrectionists”), Luke says he was jailed {lk 23:25 διὰ στάσιν καὶ φόνον} (“for insurrection and murder”), and John calls him a {jn 18:40 λῃστής}, a word Josephus uses for armed rebels. The irony is sharp: Jesus is crucified as a would-be king, and a real insurrectionist goes free.

sections.heading: Jesus Barabbas
sections.body: In Matthew, Pilate asks {mt 27:17 Ἰησοῦν τὸν Βαραββᾶν ἢ Ἰησοῦν τὸν λεγόμενον χριστόν} (“Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus called Christ?”). Most manuscripts lack the first “Jesus”, but the third-century scholar Origen knew copies that had it, and disliked the idea of a sinner bearing the holy name. That is exactly why scribes might have removed it, and most modern editions now print it. In Aramaic *Bar-abba* means “son of the father”, so the crowd chooses between two sons of the father.

sections.heading: Moving the blame
sections.body:
**Mark**: Pilate knows the priests acted {mk 15:10 διὰ φθόνον} (“out of envy”), but releases Barabbas {mk 15:15 βουλόμενος τῷ ὄχλῳ τὸ ἱκανὸν ποιῆσαι} (“wishing to satisfy the crowd”). The phrase translates the Latin *satis facere*.

**Matthew**: Pilate's wife warns him after a dream; Pilate washes his hands, {mt 27:24 Ἀθῷός εἰμι ἀπὸ τοῦ αἵματος} (“I am innocent of this blood”), and {mt 27:25 πᾶς ὁ λαὸς} (“all the people”) take the blood on themselves and their children.

**Luke**: Pilate declares Jesus innocent three times and finally hands him over {lk 23:25 τῷ θελήματι αὐτῶν} (“to their will”).

**John**: the chief priests declare {jn 19:15 Οὐκ ἔχομεν βασιλέα εἰ μὴ Καίσαρα} (“we have no king but Caesar”), which in John's terms amounts to renouncing God's kingship.

sections.heading: History and its aftermath
sections.body:
Outside the Gospels, Philo and Josephus portray Pilate as stubborn and brutal, not as a vacillating man pushed around by a crowd. Many historians therefore read the Gospels' increasingly sympathetic Pilate as reflecting the needs of Christians who lived under Rome and were in conflict with synagogues. Others reply that a governor facing a festival crowd, and wary of complaints reaching Rome, could well have hesitated as the Gospels describe.

Matthew 27:25 was later used to brand Jews collectively as “Christ-killers”, a charge that fueled centuries of persecution. The Catholic Church formally rejected it at the Second Vatican Council (*Nostra Aetate*, 1965), and most churches and New Testament scholars today read the verse within Matthew's own setting, a bitter dispute inside the Jewish community of the first century.

deep.lede: The Gospels describe the act of crucifixion in a single verb, {mk 15:24 καὶ σταυροῦσιν αὐτὸν} (“and they crucify him”), told in Mark's vivid present tense. Their attention goes elsewhere: to scripture, especially Psalm 22, to the mockers, to the placard over his head, and to the people who stood nearby.

sections.heading: Psalm 22 as a script
sections.body:
The details Mark chooses follow Psalm 22 closely. The soldiers {mk 15:24 διαμερίζονται τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ βάλλοντες κλῆρον} (“divide his garments, casting lots”), from Psalm 22:18. The passers-by mock him {mk 15:29 κινοῦντες τὰς κεφαλὰς αὐτῶν} (“shaking their heads”), from Psalm 22:7. Mark never says “this fulfilled the scripture”; he lets the allusions speak for themselves.

John quotes the psalm outright, {jn 19:24 Διεμερίσαντο τὰ ἱμάτιά μου ἑαυτοῖς} (“they divided my garments among them”), and then does something like what Matthew did with the donkeys. He takes the psalm's two parallel lines as two separate events: the garments are divided into four shares, and the seamless tunic is assigned by lot {jn 19:23 τὸν χιτῶνα} (“the tunic”).

sections.heading: The mockers
sections.body:
In Mark everyone mocks him: passers-by, chief priests and scribes, and both men crucified with him. The priests' taunt is truer than they know: {mk 15:31 Ἄλλους ἔσωσεν ἑαυτὸν οὐ δύναται σῶσαι} (“he saved others; he cannot save himself”). In Mark's theology, that is precisely the point.

Luke separates the people from their leaders. {lk 23:35 εἱστήκει ὁ λαὸς θεωρῶν} (“the people stood **watching**”); only the rulers sneer. Only one criminal mocks, {lk 23:39 σῶσον σεαυτὸν καὶ ἡμᾶς} (“save yourself and us”), while the other asks to be remembered and receives the promise of Paradise.

sections.heading: The placard
sections.body: The charge is worded differently in each Gospel. Mark's is shortest: {mk 15:26 Ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων} (“The King of the Jews”). John's is longest, {jn 19:19 Ἰησοῦς ὁ Ναζωραῖος ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων} (“Jesus the Nazorean, the King of the Jews”); in Latin it gave Christian art the initials INRI. John alone says it was written in three languages and that Pilate refused to change it: {jn 19:22 Ὃ γέγραφα γέγραφα} (“what I have written, I have written”). Pilate becomes an unwitting herald of the kingship he has just condemned.

sections.heading: Who stood near the cross
sections.body: In the Synoptics the women watch {mk 15:40 ἀπὸ μακρόθεν} (“from a distance”). John places a small group {jn 19:25 παρὰ τῷ σταυρῷ} (“beside the cross”): Jesus' mother, her sister, Mary of Clopas, Mary Magdalene, and the Beloved Disciple. To them Jesus says {jn 19:26 Γύναι ἴδε ὁ υἱός σου} (“Woman, here is your son”). Neither Jesus' mother nor the Beloved Disciple appears at the cross in any other Gospel. Interpreters have read the scene as a founding of the new family of believers, which is a theme throughout John.
